newsitem.title: FRANCE: New Beaujolais wine flows freely in annual rite.
newsitem.headline: New Beaujolais wine flows freely in annual rite.

text.p: Corks popped around the globe on Thursday to celebrate the release of 1996 Beaujolais Nouveau, the much-hyped young wine that has made a sharp comeback after last year's boycott over French nuclear testing.

From Tokyo to Maputo, Damascus to New York, Cuba to the Fiji Islands, the wine began flowing just after the stroke of midnight on Wednesday in an annual rite that has become a yuppy tradition around the world.
While Beaujolais Nouveau will be exported this year to more than 190 countries, France remains its most faithful fan, with fully half of production destined for domestic consumption.

"Here in France, the new Beaujolais is always very popular. It gives us a chance to celebrate wine by drinking a glass together with old friends," said Nicolas Laurent, a Paris wine merchant offering free samples of several different makers' products at a busy Paris market.
"In general I prefer beer, but this was free. I especially liked the second one, it was great," customer Anatole Lombard of Paris told Laurent after sampling several different bottles.
"I can't remember which is which, but it tastes like raspberries," said Rebecca Wade, a London musician performing this month in a Paris opera production.

An informal consumer boycott, launched after France's final series of six nuclear tests, which ended in January, had cut deeply into last year's Beaujolais sales, particularly in the Nordic states, Australia and Japan.
Eighteen percent less of the wine was sold in 1995 than the previous year, prompting some wine professionals to predict the boycott marked the beginning of the end for the trendy drink.
Beaujolais makers feared consumers would try some of the lower-priced, high-quality imitations from Australia, Chili and California and never return to the original.
Instead, advance sales rebounded sharply this year, ensuring that the Beaujolais tradition would survive at least one more year.
"We've got back orders -- people ordering it before it came in," said Max Zimmerman, owner of one of Chicago's largest wine retailers.
"But the Nouveaux haven't been selling as well as they used to," he added. "It's not the taste, it's just that people don't care about it anymore".
France's central Beaujolais region nonetheless produced 53 million bottles of the wine this year, up from 47 million bottles last year, according to the Beaujolais Wine Board.
About half of that was destined for export, with Germany, Switzerland, the United States, Great Britain and the Netherlands the biggest buyers, based on 1995 sales figures.
Even Moscow has been touched by the phenomenon, with a five-star hotel in the Russian capital offering an $80 buffet dinner with a free flow of Beaujolais Nouveau.
Ironically, growers all but wrote off the new vintage in August when heavy rains threatened to trigger a bad outbreak of rot.
But two weeks of cool sunshine in early September saved the crop, earning it the nickname "the miracle vintage".
"An ample ripening of the grapes has given the wines a supple texture and vivaciousness, with aromas of raspberries, wild strawberries and peaches," was how one expert assessed the new wine.
